text: Lesson 5 established the deployment order. This lesson turns that order into real commands — a resource group, then a VNet or VPC, then subnets — and covers the one planning decision that's easy to get wrong on a first deployment: how big to size the address block before you ever carve a single subnet out of it.

In Azure, az group create makes the resource group, az network vnet create makes the VNet with its first subnet in the same call, and az network vnet subnet create adds each additional one. A 10.0.0.0/16 VNet split into 10.0.1.0/24 and 10.0.2.0/24 gives a web tier and an app tier their own isolated subnets, ready for the NSGs the next lesson attaches to them.

AWS follows the identical shape with different commands: aws ec2 create-vpc for the overall block, then aws ec2 create-subnet once per subnet, each one pinned to a specific availability zone. Same 10.0.0.0/16 VPC, same web and app split — just a different CLI producing the same real network plan taught in the earlier Azure and AWS networking courses.

The planning question isn't how many addresses you need today — it's how many subnets this environment will have a year from now. A /16 split into a handful of /24s only uses a small slice of that space, deliberately leaving the rest reserved for a monitoring tier, a backup subnet, or a second availability zone added later. Size it too tight at /24 from the start and there's no room left without a disruptive redesign.

Listing what actually deployed, with az network vnet subnet list or aws ec2 describe-subnets, confirms the ranges and availability zones are right before anything else attaches to them. Next up: deploying the NSGs and security groups that sit on top of these subnets, written correctly from the start instead of rules that are "temporarily" wide open.
